# Conclusions

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## What to take away

### Least squares

Fast, and everyone understands it. It gives you a fit and a starting point for everything else, and nothing about how sure you should be

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Maximum likelihood

Rests on a probability model for the data, so it gives you intervals and lets you compare models. It costs you a choice of that probability model and an optimiser to look after

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Bayesian inference and MCMC

- Priors put your assumptions on the table, where they can be checked
- The posterior is the whole answer: estimates, credible intervals and predictions all come from the same samples
- The Metropolis algorithm is a few lines of code. The effort goes into tuning it and checking the chains
- Never trust a chain you have not looked at

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Beyond that

Particle filters, ABC and ensembles handle stochastic models, missing likelihoods and model uncertainty. They need more expertise and more computing than anything we did today

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Which method, when

- A quick look at the data: least squares
- A result for a report: maximum likelihood
- A model with many parameters, or prior knowledge you want to use: Bayesian inference
- A stochastic model, or estimates that must update in real time: particle filtering
- A model whose likelihood you cannot write: ABC

Whatever the problem, [start simple and add complexity only when the simple version fails you]{style="color: tomato;"}

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## A last thought

Fitting a model well takes three things at once: knowledge of the disease and the setting, statistical care, and the patience to check everything

The fit is never the point. The point is to understand how the disease spreads, to predict what happens next, and to give the people making decisions something they can rely on

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Resources

### Full courses (free)

-   Model fitting and inference for infectious disease dynamics by Sebastian Funk, Anton Camacho, Helen Johnson, Amanda Minter, Kathleen O'Reilly and Nicholas Davies. [Link](https://sbfnk.github.io/mfiidd/index.html)

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Core concepts

-   [Introduction to the Concept of Likelihood and Its Applications](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/2515245917744314)
-   *Key considerations for model fitting and calibration*: [Choices and trade-offs in inference with infectious disease models](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1755436519300441?via%3Dihub)
-   *A compilation of model fitting tutorials*: [Tooling-up for infectious disease transmission modelling](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1755436520300220)

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Least squares

-   *Key tutorial on the least squares method*: [Fitting dynamic models to epidemic outbreaks with quantified uncertainty: A primer for parameter uncertainty, identifiability, and forecasts](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2468042717300234)
-   [Fitting Epidemic Models to Data by James Holland Jones](https://web.stanford.edu/class/earthsys214/notes/fit.html)

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### MLE

-   [Fitting Epidemic Models to Data by James Holland Jones](https://web.stanford.edu/class/earthsys214/notes/fit.html)
